questions.q: Which property is the defining feature that makes a controlled process a Markov decision process?
choices: The reward is always positive
The next state and reward depend only on the current state and action, not on the full history
Every action is available in every state
The discount factor equals 1
questions.explain: The Markov property is that the transition $P(s'\mid s,a)$ and reward $R(s,a)$ depend only on the current state-action pair, not on how you arrived. That memorylessness is exactly what lets a single value function summarize the future.

questions.q: In a state $s$ with action $a$, the transition row is $P(s_1\mid s,a)=0.3$, $P(s_2\mid s,a)=0.5$. If these are the only reachable states besides $s$ itself, what must $P(s\mid s,a)$ equal?
questions.explain: Each row $P(\cdot\mid s,a)$ is a probability distribution over next states, so it must sum to $1$. Here $0.3+0.5=0.8$, leaving $P(s\mid s,a)=1-0.8=0.2$.

questions.q: Select every statement that is true about policies in a finite discounted MDP.
choices: A deterministic stationary policy is a map π: S → A
Fixing a policy turns the MDP into an ordinary Markov chain with kernel P^π
A stochastic policy assigns a probability distribution π(a|s) over actions
Every policy must change its action choice over time to be useful
questions.explain: A deterministic stationary policy is a state-to-action map; a stochastic one gives a distribution over actions per state; and once a policy is fixed the MDP reduces to the Markov chain $P^\pi(s'\mid s)=\sum_a\pi(a\mid s)P(s'\mid s,a)$. Statement 4 is false — for discounted MDPs a single stationary (time-invariant) policy is optimal.

questions.q: A state $s$ self-loops to itself with probability 1 under policy π, earning reward $R=1$ every step, with discount $\gamma=0.9$. What is $V^\pi(s)$?
questions.explain: The return is the geometric series $\sum_{t\ge 0}\gamma^t\cdot 1 = \frac{1}{1-\gamma} = \frac{1}{1-0.9}=10$. Equivalently the Bellman expectation equation $V^\pi(s)=1+0.9\,V^\pi(s)$ solves to $V^\pi(s)=10$.

questions.q: Compute one Bellman-expectation backup. Action $a$ in state $s$ has $R(s,a)=5$ and goes to $s'_1$ with prob $0.8$ and $s'_2$ with prob $0.2$. The current value estimates are $V(s'_1)=10$, $V(s'_2)=0$, and $\gamma=0.9$. What is $Q^\pi(s,a)=R+\gamma\sum P\cdot V$?
Why does the policy-evaluation linear system $(I-\gamma P^\pi)V^\pi = R^\pi$ have a unique solution for a finite MDP with $\gamma<1$?
choices: Because $P^\pi$ is symmetric
Because $\gamma<1$ and $P^\pi$ is stochastic, so $I-\gamma P^\pi$ is invertible
Because $R^\pi$ is always nonnegative
Because there is only one policy
questions.explain: A stochastic matrix has spectral radius $1$, so $\gamma P^\pi$ has spectral radius $\le\gamma<1$; hence $I-\gamma P^\pi$ is invertible and $V^\pi=(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}R^\pi$ is the unique solution.

questions.q: How does the Bellman optimality equation differ from the Bellman expectation equation?
choices: It replaces the discount γ with 1
It replaces the policy-weighted average over actions with a maximum over actions
It drops the transition probabilities
It removes the reward term
questions.explain: The expectation equation averages over the policy's action distribution; the optimality equation takes $\max_a$ instead: $V^*(s)=\max_a\{R(s,a)+\gamma\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)V^*(s')\}$. The max is what makes it nonlinear.

questions.q: Once $Q^*(s,a)$ is known, how do you extract an optimal policy?
choices: Pick the action that minimizes $Q^*(s,a)$
Pick any action uniformly at random
Act greedily: $\pi^*(s)\in\arg\max_a Q^*(s,a)$
Average all actions weighted by $Q^*$
questions.explain: A greedy policy with respect to the optimal action-values is optimal: $\pi^*(s)\in\arg\max_a Q^*(s,a)$. (We maximize because rewards are being accumulated.)

questions.q: Select every statement that holds for a finite discounted MDP.
choices: There always exists a deterministic stationary optimal policy
An optimal policy is optimal from every start state simultaneously
The Bellman optimality equation is linear in V*
V*(s) = max over policies of V^π(s)
questions.explain: Finite discounted MDPs admit a deterministic stationary optimal policy that is optimal from every state, and $V^*(s)=\max_\pi V^\pi(s)$ by definition. Statement 3 is false: the $\max_a$ makes the optimality equation nonlinear (it has a kink), which is why a matrix inverse does not solve it.

questions.q: Why does value iteration $V_{k+1}=TV_k$ converge to a unique fixed point from any starting $V_0$?
choices: Because $T$ is linear
Because $T$ is a γ-contraction in the sup-norm, so the Banach fixed-point theorem applies
Because $V_0$ must be chosen as $V^*$
Because the state space is infinite
questions.explain: $T$ satisfies $\|TU-TV\|_\infty\le\gamma\|U-V\|_\infty$ with $\gamma<1$, a contraction on the complete space $(\mathbb R^{|S|},\|\cdot\|_\infty)$. Banach's theorem then gives a unique fixed point ($V^*$) and convergence from any seed.

questions.q: Value iteration starts with $\|V_0 - V^*\|_\infty = 10$ and $\gamma = 0.9$. The guaranteed bound is $\|V_k - V^*\|_\infty \le \gamma^k\|V_0-V^*\|_\infty$. What is the bound after $k=2$ steps?
questions.explain: $\gamma^k\,\|V_0-V^*\|_\infty = 0.9^2\cdot 10 = 0.81\cdot 10 = 8.1$. The error shrinks geometrically by a factor of $\gamma$ each backup.

questions.q: How does the discount factor $\gamma$ affect the convergence rate of value iteration?
choices: Larger γ (closer to 1) makes convergence faster
Larger γ (closer to 1) makes convergence slower
γ has no effect on the rate
Convergence only happens when γ = 1
questions.explain: The per-step error contracts by the factor $\gamma$, so the rate is $\gamma^k$. As $\gamma\to 1$ the contraction weakens toward $1$ and convergence slows dramatically — the price of caring about the distant future.

questions.q: What two steps make up one round of policy iteration?
choices: Random restart, then gradient descent
Policy evaluation (solve V^π), then policy improvement (greedy w.r.t. V^π)
Sort states, then prune actions
Take a single Bellman backup, then normalize
questions.explain: Each round exactly evaluates the current policy ($V^\pi=(I-\gamma P^\pi)^{-1}R^\pi$), then improves it by acting greedily with respect to that value. Repeat until the policy stops changing.

questions.q: Why does policy iteration terminate in finitely many rounds at an exactly optimal policy?
choices: Because it only converges in the limit, like value iteration
Because each round strictly improves the policy and there are only finitely many deterministic policies
Because γ must equal 0
Because the value function is always 0
questions.explain: The policy improvement theorem guarantees $V^{\pi_{k+1}}\ge V^{\pi_k}$ with strict improvement until the policy is greedy w.r.t. its own value (hence optimal). With only $|A|^{|S|}$ deterministic policies, a strictly improving sequence must stop after finitely many rounds.

questions.q: Select every correct contrast between value iteration and policy iteration.
choices: Value iteration does cheap inexact backups and converges geometrically in the limit
Policy iteration does an expensive exact evaluation each round but converges in finitely many rounds
Both are instances of generalized policy iteration
Policy iteration can never reach the optimal policy
questions.explain: Value iteration repeats cheap one-step backups, converging only in the limit at rate $\gamma^k$; policy iteration solves an exact linear system per round but converges in a small finite number of rounds. Both are points on the generalized-policy-iteration spectrum. Statement 4 is false — policy iteration terminates exactly at $\pi^*$.

questions.q: For a discount factor $\gamma = 0.95$, what is the effective horizon $1/(1-\gamma)$ (in steps)?
questions.explain: $\frac{1}{1-\gamma}=\frac{1}{1-0.95}=\frac{1}{0.05}=20$. Rewards much beyond about $20$ steps contribute almost nothing to the discounted return.

questions.q: What is the main qualitative difference between the optimal policy of a finite-horizon MDP and that of an infinite-horizon discounted MDP?
choices: The finite-horizon optimal policy is generally time-dependent (nonstationary)
The finite-horizon MDP has no optimal policy
The discounted MDP requires a different reward at each state
There is no difference
questions.explain: With a fixed number $N$ of steps remaining, the best action depends on how many steps are left (solved by backward induction $V_n$), so the optimal policy is time-dependent. In the infinite-horizon discounted case a single stationary policy is optimal.

questions.q: The average-reward objective $\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\mathbb E[\sum_{t=0}^{N-1}R_t]$ is best described as:
choices: The same as the discounted objective with γ = 0
The γ → 1 limit, used when no natural discounting exists
Always equal to the total undiscounted reward
Only defined for deterministic MDPs
questions.explain: Average-reward optimizes the per-step gain and is the $\gamma\to 1$ limiting regime; it is used when the process runs indefinitely with no natural discount. The plain undiscounted sum $\sum_t R_t$ diverges, which is why the per-step average (and its own gain–bias Bellman machinery) is needed.
